title: The king in a busy position
outcomes: Names the piece on a given square before using its rule, with no hint in the prompt
Taps every square the king can step to, removing squares next to the enemy king and squares attacked by enemy pieces
Decides whether an enemy piece next to the king can be taken, by checking whether it is defended
Ignores distant enemy pieces that attack none of the king's neighbouring squares

steps.text: In **The queen and the king** you were told "king". Now nobody says it. Name the piece first, then list its up to eight neighbouring squares and cross out the unsafe ones: squares next to the enemy king, squares an enemy piece attacks, and enemy pieces that are defended. What remains is the answer.

steps.caption: The piece on d3 is a king. The rook on e1 attacks the e-file, and the black king covers c4 and d4.

line.say: The king steps to c3, one of three safe squares.

steps.text: List the king's neighbours, then ask three questions of each: is it my own piece, is it next to the enemy king, is it attacked? An enemy piece on a neighbouring square can be taken only if nothing defends it. A far-away enemy piece matters only if it attacks one of those squares. *Rule of thumb:* check the defenders of a piece before taking it.

steps.title: Defended or not
steps.prompt: Predict first. In the first position the knight next to the king has no defender. In the second, a pawn has been added. In the third, a rook has moved far away. What does each change do to the king's squares?
In the silent items, which squares did you cross out first: the ones next to the enemy king or the ones attacked by a piece? Did you ever forget a defender?
